(Today through Monday)...
Issued at 236 AM EST Tue Nov 10 2026

Dry and mild weather will continue through the first part of 
Wednesday. Low pressure will track quickly across the Ohio Valley 
late Wednesday with showers and a few thunderstorms accompanying a 
cold front. In its wake...a cold continental airmass will spill into 
the region as a deep upper level trough expands across the eastern 
half of the country. Chilly temperatures are expected with the 
chance for scattered light precipitation Thursday and Friday. As the 
upper trough moves away to the east over the weekend...dry and 
seasonable weather will return.

Today through Wednesday Night

Quiet conditions continue this morning with clear skies under broad 
high pressure. 07Z temperatures were generally in the 40s with light 
southwest winds.

A weak frontal boundary currently across the Great Lakes will move 
south across the forecast area later today but will have little to 
no impact on sensible weather. Little moisture is present along the 
boundary with a shift to W/NW winds serving as the only signal of 
its passage from mid morning into the early afternoon. The front 
also will not take away from what will be another superb mid Fall 
day with temperatures well into the 60s. Skies will remain clear 
initially this evening but mid and high level clouds will increase 
predawn Wednesday as a compact low pressure system moves into the 
upper Mississippi Valley. Even despite the increase in higher 
clouds...light and variable winds tonight will present a greater 
potential for areas of fog to develop with the greatest risk likely 
to exist over our northeast counties.

Southerly flow will increase quickly on Wednesday as a sharp wave 
aloft associated with the surface wave approaches from the 
northwest. A narrow axis of subtly higher dewpoints will be drawn 
poleward along the attendant cold front and will approach the Wabash 
Valley by mid to late afternoon. Surface heating will promote weak 
instability with MLCAPEs rising to around 500 j/kg which should 
promote a gradually increasing but broken line of convection by late 
day that will shift across the area into the evening. The best 
instability will remain closer to the Ohio River extending north 
into far southern portions of the forecast area. Cannot rule out 
isolated stronger wind gusts with a few cells in these areas 
considering modest BL shear values peaking near 50kts...but poor 
lapse rates will serve as an overall limiting factor. Showers will 
shift to the east Wednesday night with the front...followed by 
noticeably colder air in the post frontal airmass as cold advection 
commences in concert with gusty northwest winds.

Temps...despite the passage of the weak front today...low level 
thermals support highs warming into the mid 60s and across southern 
parts of the forecast temps rising potentially into the upper 60s. 
Wednesday will remain mild ahead of the approaching surface low and 
cold front...with low to mid 60s anticipated. 

Thursday through Friday Night

The coldest air of the Fall so far arrives for the latter part of 
the week as the upper trough amplifies and settles over the eastern 
part of the country. A sharp shortwave will pivot around the flank 
of the parent trough on Thursday and interact with strong cold 
advection and steepening mid level lapse rates to generate scattered 
to numerous light rain showers focused especially across the 
northeast half of the forecast area. The addition of brisk northwest 
winds and broad stratus will make for a raw and unpleasant day 
across the area with highs likely to hold in the 40s. 

Subtle ridging Thursday evening will aid in decreasing shower 
coverage but yet another shortwave will pivot across the region 
Friday morning which will maintain at least a broken stratus deck 
with the potential for renewed light precipitation. A more 
pronounced northerly fetch off Lake Michigan early Friday supports 
the development of a more persistent north-south band of rain and 
snow that may be able to briefly make it as far south as the 
northern Wabash Valley Friday morning before low level flow backs 
and any lingering precipitation shifts east and decreases in 
response to a weakening NW-SE flow off the lake. Low clouds will 
slowly decrease from the west Friday night as the upper low swings 
into the eastern Great Lakes and drier air begins to advect in from 
the west. Low level thermals on Friday suggest 45 degrees is 
probably the upper limit for a high and there is potential for much 
of the northeast half of the forecast area to not make it out of the 
lower 40s. This will set the stage for the coldest night of the Fall 
so far Friday night with a hard freeze for the entire area as lows 
fall into the mid 20s.
